To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the AGASA and Fly’s Eye experiments have set new bounds on the flux of ultra-high energy neutrinos from astrophysical sources, and on the cross sections for neutrinos to produce black holes and other exotic particles in collisions with nucleons, with implications for the fundamental Planck and GUT scales.

the Fly’s Eye and AGASA collaborations have combined their data to derive the most stringent limits to date on the production of ultra-high energy cosmic neutrino-induced showers in the atmosphere, and have thereby placed model-dependent and model-independent bounds that improve upon existing limits.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the physics of neutrino interactions with matter.
the study of the interactions of ultra-high energy (UHE) neutrinos with matter.
two major topics in astrophysics: (1) ultra-high energy cosmic neutrino astronomy; and (2) the fundamental Planck-scale in models with extra dimensions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the non-observation of UHE neutrinos by the Fly’s Eye and AGASA implies that the neutrino cross section is less than or equal to a certain value, which depends on the astrophysical model and new physics model.
ultra-high energy cosmic neutrino searches have already provided a wealth of information about both astrophysical source models and new physics.
the non-observation of UHECRs with energy above the GZK limit rules out the possibility of the existence of neutrinos in the energy range 10 18 eV to 10 19 eV.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the absence of ultra-high energy cosmic rays implies the absence of ultra high-energy cosmic neutrinos.
we have set the most restrictive bounds to date in all cases.
we have derived the strongest constraints to date on new physics from the nonobservation of ultra-high energy neutrinos.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, despite the large exposure of the Fly's Eye, the current generation of cosmic ray detectors is not yet capable of probing the neutrino flux expected from the highest energy cosmic ray sources.
ultra-high energy neutrinos are powerful probes of astrophysical sources, new physics, and the early universe.
the next generation of ground-based detectors will be able to test the standard model of neutrino cross sections and to constrain astrophysical flux models.
